tagline.text: A 140 m-wide curtain of water seeping from an entire cliff face

location.label: Location
location.text: Sitio Dulao, Upper Dado, Alamada, North Cotabato

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱900~1,500 (per person, day trip from Cotabato City)

children.text: Water seeps from an entire rock cliff about 60 m high and forms a green curtain roughly 140 m wide. With no river above it, the sight of water welling out of the cliff is unique, and you can combine a short stair trek down with a dip in cold water.

Asik-Asik Falls is in Sitio Dulao, Barangay Upper Dado, Alamada, North Cotabato. Tucked into a deep valley on the slopes of Mount Ragang, it became known in late 2010 when a barangay councilor found it while assessing damage from forest fires, landslides and floods. Villagers are said to have known about it earlier, but the forest was so dense that outsiders could hardly reach it.
What makes the falls special is that no river feeds them from above. The highest drop is about
and the total width is about

, and water trickles down through the cracks of the whole rock face, which is covered in moss, ferns and vines so that it looks like a green curtain. Many people guess the source is groundwater or an underground river, but this has not been confirmed. In Hiligaynon, "asik" means to sprinkle or splash, so "asik-asik" is loosely understood as "sprinkling down."

In July 2013, a photo of the falls won the grand prize in a photo contest held by the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR), which made it known nationwide. Since then the local government has improved the roads, bridges, viewing areas and concrete stairs, and today it is a leading attraction of the Cotabato area that anyone can reach by stairs. The Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) is recorded as having surveyed the site in 2019 and recommended declaring it a national geological monument.

That said, it is not an easy place to reach. Even from Cotabato City or Kidapawan, the last stretch means riding a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) up a mountain road, and getting to the bottom of the falls means walking down several hundred steps and back up again. In return, if you go early in the morning when few people are around, you can enjoy the valley in front of the falls almost as if you had it to yourself, so it is worth giving the trip a full day.

blocks.title: Curtain waterfall seeping from the cliff

children.text: Instead of a single stream, water runs down through the cracks of a cliff about
wide. Because there is no river above it, locals also call it the "miracle falls." Standing in front of it, you can feel the mist on your face.

blocks.title: Wall of green moss and ferns

children.text: The cliff the water runs down is covered with moss, ferns and vines, so the brown rock, green plants and white water form layers. Many reviews say photos look best when the morning sun reaches the falls.
A concrete staircase follows the ravine, and there are viewing sections on the way down where you can see the whole falls from above. The number of steps differs between guides; many say about
400 steps
, though some reviewers say that counting them yourself gives more.

You can dip your feet or play in the shallow water that flows out from the base of the falls. The water is very cold and clear, which is great for cooling off. The rocks are slippery, so you need aqua shoes or sandals.

blocks.title: Countryside on the slopes of Mount Ragang

children.text: On the habal-habal ride up, you can see rice fields, coconut palms and mountain villages. The road surface has improved, but some stretches are still bumpy, so the ride itself becomes part of the trip.
Along the same road there are small resorts such as Portalio Coldspring and Salukot Mountain View Resort, and more adventurous travelers can continue by trekking to Daday Falls or Palepaz Falls.
The entrance fee is very low, and habal-habal drivers, snack stalls and simple huts provide income for local residents. Using local habal-habal and buying snacks is the best way to support them.

items.title: Day trip from Cotabato City
items.subtitle: An itinerary by bus and habal-habal

children.text: Take a bus or van bound for Libungan from the bus terminal in Cotabato City. It takes about
1 hour
, and one guide listed the fare as about
At the habal-habal stand near Libungan Public Market, negotiate a round trip to the falls. One guide gives about
for two people, and you should expect about
1 hour
each way. Agree on the return time in advance.
Pay the entrance fee at the gate and ask the staff about current operating conditions. Check your water, snacks and cash here.
Walk down the stairs. The descent takes about
15~30 minutes
, so go slowly and take photos at the viewing sections on the way.
Enjoy the stream in front of the falls and take photos. Early morning, before the crowds arrive, is best, and a waterproof pouch gives peace of mind.
The climb back up takes about
30~45 minutes
. There are several places to rest, so stop whenever you are out of breath.
Have lunch at a stall near the entrance or a nearby eatery, then take a habal-habal back to Libungan.
In Libungan, check the time of the last ride to Cotabato City and board a bus or van.
Bus schedules and habal-habal fares vary with the season and local conditions, so it is a good idea to check once more with your lodging staff the day before you leave.

items.title: Two-day trip from Davao
items.subtitle: One night in Kidapawan or Midsayap

children.text: Take a Cotabato-bound bus from a terminal such as Ecoland Terminal in Davao to Kidapawan or Midsayap. One guide says it takes about
3.5~4 hours
to reach Midsayap.
Drop your bags at your lodging and, if you are in Kidapawan, take a light look around nearby spots such as Lake Agco and the geothermal springs.
Head out from your lodging to Alamada town proper or the Upper Dado entrance. One guide says it takes about
1.5~2 hours
from Kidapawan, so an early start is needed.
Find a habal-habal in Alamada and ride up to the falls entrance. Pay the entrance fee and walk down the stairs.
Spend two to three hours at the falls taking photos and playing in the water, then climb back up.
After lunch, return to your base city and take a bus to Davao.
We do not recommend a day trip from Davao to the falls because the travel is long. Sleeping one night in a base city is far more comfortable.
Fly from Manila to Cotabato Airport (CBO) or Davao Airport (DVO). Routes and flight frequencies change by airline, so check before booking.
From Cotabato Airport, take a taxi or tricycle into the city and then look for a ride to Libungan.
If you enter through Davao, the overland leg is long, so it is better to add a night before or after the falls.
There is no direct transport from Manila to the falls. Allow at least a day for flights and overland travel combined.
Take a bus or van from Cotabato City to Libungan Public Market. One guide gave the fare as about
and the travel time as about
1 hour
In Libungan, negotiate a habal-habal directly to the falls. One guide gives about
round trip for two people, and the ride is about
1 hour
each way.
For a cheaper route, you can take a jeepney from Libungan to Alamada (about
1.5 hours
) and find a habal-habal there, but it takes longer.
From Davao, take a Cotabato-bound bus or van and get off at the Midsayap or Libungan junction. Tell the driver in advance that you are going to Asik-Asik Falls.
One guide says it takes about
1.5~2 hours
from Kidapawan, and for a day trip a chartered van or private car is more convenient.
You can also take a habal-habal from Midsayap, and one guide gives about
round trip for two people (negotiable).
From the entrance you go on foot down the stairs. Habal-habal only go as far as the entrance.
Agree with the driver on the times for going and returning, and settle the price before you set off.

The dry season from November to April is best. During this period the mountain road is less muddy and the stairs are less slippery. One guide also recommends the dry season and says heavy rain makes the road slippery and access difficult.

In the rainy season the water may rise and look more majestic, but the stairs and stream are very slippery, and entry may be restricted for safety during heavy rain. In any season the heat builds after noon, so it is best to reach the falls in the morning.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The best time for trekking. Local visitors increase on weekends.
An early start is essential. Good for playing in the stream.
The stairs and mountain road are slippery. Change your plans if heavy rain is forecast.

There is almost no lodging near the falls, so most people stay in Kidapawan, Midsayap or Cotabato City and travel out. Kidapawan has several mid-range hotels and inns, and Midsayap also has a boutique hotel. One guide mentions homestays run by villagers, but contacts and rates change often, so check the latest information.

For meals, rely on stalls at the falls entrance or Libungan market. Reviews mention local snacks such as pastel (a local chicken-and-rice dish) and boiled eggs being sold, but the menu varies day to day. There are almost no eateries inside the falls area, so bring plenty of water and snacks.
If you set off between
and
and reach the falls before
, there are fewer people and the light is good.
Wear aqua shoes or non-slip sandals. The stairs and stream rocks are very slippery.
One guide says there are almost no ATMs or card payments there, so bring plenty of cash in pesos.
There is a lot of mist, so it is a good idea to keep your camera and phone in a waterproof pouch.
Settle the habal-habal fare before you leave, including the round trip and waiting time.
The climb back up is the hardest part. If you are not very fit, go up slowly with rests, and bring enough water.
Always carry your trash out. It is a protected area, so do not leave plastic or wrappers behind.
Before visiting, check operating hours and whether reservations are required with the Alamada municipal office or tourism office.
Security conditions differ by area around Cotabato, so be sure to check your government's travel advisory and the latest local notices before you depart.
After heavy rain the stairs and mountain road are slippery and the stream level can rise suddenly, so do not push yourself.

A 2020 guide (vismin.ph) listed pre-booking on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., while another guide lists daily hours of 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. with no reservation mentioned, and some visitors report registering at the jump-off point before the walk. One guide also noted a temporary closure, so confirm the current rules with the Alamada tourism office before you visit.
Several hundred steps each way can be a burden for people with weak knees or hearts, children and the elderly.
Plan your day so you are back before dark, and avoid traveling on mountain roads at night.
Entrance fees, step counts and operating rules differ between sources, so check the latest information.
The highest peak in the Philippines, approached from Kidapawan. It is common to combine it with the falls by staying one night in Kidapawan.
